extracted.intended_audience: students, scientists, and philosophers learning scientific method and critical reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and distinguish principal kinds of fallacies that occur in scientific and philosophical reasoning, with examples and guidance for detecting them (especially a priori errors and suppressed premises). Useful for evaluating arguments and the soundness of inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Fallacies of Induction where the facts on which the induction proceeds are erroneous; includes malobservation, non-observation, and errors arising from intermediate marks that do not prove what they are supposed to prove.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat as a single class of all inductions in which the error lies in not sufficiently ascertaining the facts on which the theory is grounded, whether the cause be malobservation, simple non-observation, or indirect/misleading signs. Detect by checking factual bases and how observations were obtained; beware of inferences built on uncertain or misread empirical signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive fallacies in which the facts are correct but the conclusion is not warranted by them (false or overreaching generalization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs when correct observations are misconstrued or overgeneralized; examine whether the evidence actually supports the universal claim and whether alternative causes/explanations have been considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Ratiocination
rubrics_metrics.description: Fallacies of Deduction in which the premises of the ratiocination do not bear out its conclusion; essentially vicious argumentation opposed to the rules of the syllogism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on whether the logical steps legitimately follow from the premises. Even with true premises, check that distribution and middle terms are properly handled; supply suppressed steps to see if the syllogism is valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors arising from neglect or inability to state the question properly and to apprehend the evidence with definiteness and precision—includes reasoning in a circle and cases where premises were never distinctly conceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often the most obvious characteristic is confusion rather than a specific false premise; many fallacies can be (and often are) assigned here when suppressed or vague premises make classification ambiguous. Remedy by clarifying concepts and insisting on precise statement of premises and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppressed Premises / Tacit Assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: In everyday argument some links are suppressed; the erring step often lurks in tacit, half-conscious, or unconscious assumptions. To detect the fallacy, the silently assumed proposition must be supplied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic/peer-reviewer must attempt to infer or elicit the suppressed premise (Socratic interrogation). Be aware that supplying different plausible suppressed premises can reclassify the fallacy (e.g., as false premise vs. unsound syllogism). Example: arguing from 'the country's distress' to 'government is tyrannical' requires supplying either a false universal premise or an unsound syllogism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Simple Inspection; Or A Priori Fallacies
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors in which propositions are embraced as requiring no proof—accepted as self-evident or resting on intrinsic verisimilitude rather than evidence. These include many forms where the mind's structure is mistaken for facts about the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept as given propositions merely because they appear self-evident to intuition. Examine whether assumptions labelled 'a priori' are in fact grounded in experience or are unjustified extrapolations from mental habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistaking Ideas for Reality (mind→world transfer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming that the same order must obtain among objects in nature which obtains among our ideas of them—taking laws of the percipient mind for laws of the perceived object, or properties of ideas for properties of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for inference from the structure of thought to the structure of reality (e.g., because we think two things together, they must co-exist). Such moves often underlie popular superstitions and metaphysical errors; verify by seeking independent empirical support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whatever is Inconceivable Must be False
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that whatever we cannot conceive (or which is inconceivable) must be impossible or false—summarized as 'Whatever is inconceivable must be false.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conflates limits of imagination with limits of nature. Historical counterexamples include antipodes, Copernican astronomy, and Newtonian action at a distance. Peer-reviewers should not reject hypotheses merely because they seem inconceivable; instead, test them against evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Things Which We Cannot Think of Together Cannot Co-exist
rubrics_metrics.description: The related maxim that what we cannot conceive together cannot exist together; i.e., conceivability is treated as a criterion of possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using conceivability as a basis for asserting impossibility. Distinguish between genuine logical contradictions and mere imaginative difficulty; consider extension of conception with new experience and concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification of Abstractions / Whatever can be thought of apart exists apart
rubrics_metrics.description: The tendency to treat names and abstractions as distinct objective entities (e.g., treating 'whiteness' or 'man in general' as real substances). Enunciated as 'Whatever can be thought of apart exists apart.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware reification: do not assume that because language or thought distinguishes a concept there exists a separate ontological entity corresponding to it. Check whether the term denotes a linguistic convenience or a genuine distinct object requiring evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias Toward Simplicity ('nature acts by the simplest means')
rubrics_metrics.description: The axiom that 'nature always acts by the simplest means' or that the explanation most easily conceivable is likeliest to be true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity can be a heuristic but is not decisive. Historical errors (e.g., insistence on circular heavenly motions) show that assuming simplicity without empirical validation can mislead. Use Occam-like heuristics cautiously and test predictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misapplied Principle of Sufficient Reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming that because we see no reason why a phenomenon should deviate in one way rather than another, it therefore will not deviate—i.e., using the lack of an apparent reason as proof of constancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This move can be fallacious (and reducible to petitio principii); not seeing a reason for alternative behavior is not proof of its impossibility. Example: reasoning that a body at rest cannot begin to move without external force because there is 'no reason' for motion in any particular direction; this assumes what it must prove. Insist on independent evidence for claims about necessity.
